1: # User-Mode Hello Example
2: 
3: This self-contained example demonstrates the complete path from a packaged user
4: module to A32 USR mode and a custom UART syscall. Its kernel, user program,
5: shared example ABI, image manifest, and test all live in this directory so none
6: of its interfaces become part of the canonical template.
7: 
8: From the repository root:
9: 
10: ```sh
11: make user-mode-hello-image
12: make -C examples/user-mode-hello test
13: ```
14: 
15: The loader uses bounded static storage for up to 16 user image pages. The
16: example syscall writes one byte to UART0; Assignment 2 replaces it with the
17: required `ioctl` interface.

## The files and their roles

```
examples/user-mode-hello/
├── image.toml            # packaging: kernel ELF + module named "user-hello"
├── test.toml             # expected UART output + trace event
├── include/hello_syscall.h   # shared syscall ABI (kernel + user both include it)
├── kernel/
│   ├── main.c            # boot, module loader, page tables, syscall dispatcher
│   ├── user.S            # minemu_enter_user — the USR-mode transition
│   └── svc.S             # minemu_svc_trampoline — builds/restores the trap frame
└── user/
    ├── main.c            # minemu_user_main — the "hello world" program
    └── syscall.S         # minemu_hello_uart_putchar — the svc #0 stub
```

---

## 1. Loading a packaged module

The packaging is declared in `image.toml` — the tool `minemu image` bakes your kernel ELF *and* the user ELF into one disk image:

```toml
kernel = "kernel/build/user-mode-hello.elf"

[[modules]]
name = "user-hello"
elf = "user/build/user-hello.elf"
```

At boot, the bootloader hands the kernel a `minemu_boot_info` (`kernel/include/minemu/boot.h`) which contains `module_table_offset` / `module_count` — an array of `minemu_module_record`, each of which points to an array of `minemu_module_segment`. A segment is basically an ELF program header flattened into 5 fields: `data_offset` (where in the ROM image the bytes live), `virtual_address`, `file_size`, `memory_size`, `flags` (R/W/X).

The kernel side of finding it is `find_module()` in `kernel/main.c:110`. It just walks the module table comparing names byte-by-byte:

```c
static const struct minemu_module_record *find_module(...) {
    const uint8_t *image = (const uint8_t *)(uintptr_t)boot_info->system_rom_base;
    ...
    for (uint32_t index = 0; index < boot_info->module_count; ++index) {
        const struct minemu_module_record *module = &modules[index];
        if (module->name_length == name_length && ... bytes_equal(...))
            return module;
    }
}
```

Note it validates *everything* — `image_records_valid` / `image_range_valid` check that every offset+length is inside the ROM image before dereferencing. That's the pattern you'd want to keep: the module table is untrusted input.

Then `load_user_module()` (`kernel/main.c:201`) copies the segments out of ROM into static RAM:

- `prepare_user_range()` allocates a page slot per page of the segment (bounded static storage — `MAX_USER_IMAGE_PAGES 16`, so `user_image_pages[16][4096]`).
- `write_user_range()` first zeroes `memory_size`, then copies `file_size` bytes. The gap between them is your `.bss`.

```c
!write_user_range(segment->virtual_address, NULL, segment->memory_size) ||          // zero-fill bss
!write_user_range(segment->virtual_address, image + segment->data_offset,
                  segment->file_size)                                               // copy file bytes
```

It also sanity-checks that `entry_vaddr` actually lands inside an executable segment (`entry_is_executable`, line 241) — otherwise it refuses to run.

---

## 2. Creating the address space and stack

Still in `load_user_module()`, but now the MMU part:

**The page table.** There's a single static L1 table, `user_page_table[1024]`, plus one L2-ish mapping since this platform uses a flat 1MB-section directory + page tables — actually it fills in per-4KB PTEs:

```c
for (size_t index = 0; index < user_page_count; ++index) {
    uint32_t table_index = (user_page_vaddrs[index] >> 12) & 1023U;
    user_page_table[table_index] = kernel_vaddr_to_paddr(user_image_pages[index]) |
                                   MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER |
                                   user_page_flags[index];       // R/W/X from the segment
}
```

The important bit is **`MINEMU_PTE_USER`** — that's what makes the page accessible from USR mode at all. Without it, the moment you drop to user mode you'd take a permission fault.

**The stack:**

```c
user_page_table[(USER_STACK_BOTTOM >> 12) & 1023U] =
    kernel_vaddr_to_paddr(user_stack) | MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER |
    MINEMU_PTE_READABLE | MINEMU_PTE_WRITABLE;
```

One page, mapped at `USER_STACK_BOTTOM = 0x007ff000`, so the stack grows down from `USER_STACK_TOP = 0x00800000`. The backing memory is the kernel's own static `user_stack[4096]` array — user "RAM" is really just kernel BSS, aliased through the user page table.

**Hooking it into the live address space:**

```c
volatile uint32_t *directory = active_page_directory();
directory[USER_IMAGE_BASE >> 22] =
    kernel_vaddr_to_paddr(user_page_table) | MINEMU_PDE_VALID;
minemu_mmu_tlbiall();
```

The user image is at `0x00400000`, which sits in the first 1MB-aligned region of the *low* address space — deliberately below the kernel. This is the key mental model: **the kernel does not switch page tables.** It keeps running on the same active directory and simply installs the user's L1 entry into the low region. Kernel stays mapped (in the high/direct-map region), user gets the low region. One address space, two halves.

---

## 3. Entering USR mode

`minemu_kernel_main` ends with:

```c
minemu_enter_user(module->entry_vaddr, USER_STACK_TOP);
```

which is `kernel/user.S` — 20 lines of assembly doing three jobs:

**a) Seed the user's banked SP/LR.** USR mode has its own SP and LR that are banked — you can't touch them directly from SVC mode. But ARM gives you a trick: `ldmia ... {sp, lr}^` in a privileged mode writes the *user-mode banked* registers:

```asm
sub sp, sp, #8
str r1, [sp]            @ r1 = USER_STACK_TOP
mov r3, #0
str r3, [sp, #4]        @ user LR = 0
mov r3, sp
ldmia r3, {sp, lr}^     @ write USR's banked SP/LR from memory
add sp, sp, #8
```

**b) Set up the return state.** `movs pc, lr` returns using SPSR, so SPSR must describe the state you want:

```asm
mov r3, #0x10           @ 0x10 = USR mode
msr spsr_cxsf, r3       @ no Thumb bit -> A32
mov lr, r2              @ r2 = entry_vaddr -> this is the "return address"
```

**c) Drop registers and jump:**

```asm
mov r0, #0 ... mov r3, #0    @ ABI-clean entry state
movs pc, lr                   @ PC <- entry, CPSR <- SPSR(USR)
```

After `movs pc, lr` the CPU is in USR mode executing at `entry_vaddr` — which, per `user/common/user.ld`, is `__minemu_user_start`, which calls your `minemu_user_main()`.

---

## 4. The syscall round trip (where the SVC frame save/restore lives)

This is a four-step chain. Walk it with the `hello world` loop in `user/main.c`.

### Step 1 — user stub (`user/syscall.S`)

```asm
minemu_hello_uart_putchar:
    push {r7, lr}
    mov r7, #MINEMU_HELLO_SYSCALL_UART_PUTCHAR   @ syscall number in r7
    svc #0
    pop {r7, pc}
```

Conventions: **syscall number in `r7`, argument in `r0`, return value in `r0`**. The kernel's dispatcher validates exactly this.

### Step 2 — hardware enters SVC, trampoline builds the frame (`kernel/svc.S`)

On `svc #0`, the CPU (in SVC mode) jumps to the vector with `lr` = next instruction and `spsr` = the caller's CPSR. `minemu_svc_trampoline` then hand-builds an 88-byte `minemu_trap_frame` on the stack:

```asm
minemu_svc_trampoline:
    sub sp, sp, #88
    stmia sp, {r0-r12}          @ r[0..12]      offset 0
    str lr, [sp, #52]           @ return_lr     offset 52
    mrs r1, spsr
    str r1, [sp, #56]           @ spsr          offset 56
    ldr r1, =-3
    str r1, [sp, #60]           @ exception_id = SVC (-3)
    sub r1, lr, #4
    str r1, [sp, #64]           @ fault_pc = address of the svc instruction
    mov r1, #0
    str r1, [sp, #68]           @ dfsr
    str r1, [sp, #72]           @ dfar
    add r1, sp, #76
    stmia r1, {sp, lr}^         @ user_sp, user_lr   (banked USR regs)
    mov r1, #0
    str r1, [sp, #84]           @ reserved
    mov r0, sp                  @ arg0 = &frame
    bl minemu_svc_dispatch
    mov sp, r0                  @ frame the C code returns (may differ!)
```

Every offset here matches `struct minemu_trap_frame` in `kernel/include/minemu/trap.h`, which pins them with `_Static_assert`s. The `stmia r1, {sp, lr}^` is the same privileged-user-register trick from `user.S`, reading USR's banked SP/LR this time.

Note `fault_pc = lr - 4` — for SVC, `lr` points *past* the instruction, so subtracting 4 recovers the `svc #0` itself. That's what lets the dispatcher re-read the instruction.

### Step 3 — the dispatcher (`kernel/main.c:268`)

```c
struct minemu_trap_frame *minemu_svc_dispatch(struct minemu_trap_frame *frame) {
    uint32_t mode = frame->spsr & CPSR_MODE_MASK;
    if (frame->exception_id != MINEMU_EXCEPTION_SVC || mode != CPSR_MODE_USR ||
        (frame->spsr & CPSR_THUMB) != 0) {          // must really be USR, A32
        frame->r[0] = (uint32_t)MINEMU_HELLO_SYSCALL_ERROR;
        return frame;
    }

    uint32_t instruction = *(const uint32_t *)(uintptr_t)frame->fault_pc;
    if (instruction != A32_SVC_ZERO ||              // must be `svc #0`
        frame->r[7] != MINEMU_HELLO_SYSCALL_UART_PUTCHAR ||  // known call number
        frame->r[0] > UINT8_MAX) {                  // arg must be a byte
        frame->r[0] = (uint32_t)MINEMU_HELLO_SYSCALL_ERROR;
        return frame;
    }

    if (!user_syscall_observed) {
        minemu_trace_event(TRACE_USER_SYSCALL);     // 0x48454c10, once
        user_syscall_observed = true;
    }
    MINEMU_UART0->tx_data = frame->r[0];            // the actual "write"
    frame->r[0] = 0;                                // success
    return frame;
}
```

It's defensive on four axes: exception type, caller mode, exact instruction encoding, and argument range. Note it writes the return value **into the frame** (`frame->r[0] = 0`) rather than into a register directly — the frame *is* the register file.

### Step 4 — restore and return (`kernel/svc.S`)

```asm
    mov sp, r0                 @ use the frame pointer C returned
    ldr lr, [sp, #52]          @ return_lr
    ldr r1, [sp, #56]
    msr spsr_cxsf, r1          @ restore caller's CPSR (USR, flags)
    add r1, sp, #76
    ldmia r1, {sp, lr}^        @ restore USR's banked SP/LR
    ldmia sp, {r0-r12}         @ restore r0 (now 0) .. r12
    add sp, sp, #88            @ pop the frame
    movs pc, lr                @ return to USR: PC <- lr, CPSR <- spsr
```

"Save and restore the supplied SVC frame" = **the trampoline constructs the frame, hands it to C, then reverses the construction verbatim, writing back whatever C left in it.** The only thing that changes is `r0`, which is why the syscall's return value appears in user code as the C function's return value. The `movs pc, lr` both jumps back *and* reloads CPSR from SPSR, dropping privilege back to USR in the same instruction.

---

## 5. What the test proves

```toml
[assert]
uart0_contains = "hello world"
execution_lifecycle = "paused"
shutdown_lifecycle = "stopped"
trace_values = [0x48454c10]        # TRACE_USER_SYSCALL
```

"hello world" on UART0 proves the loader → address space → USR entry → syscall → dispatch → restore chain all worked. The trace value proves user code actually executed at least one syscall (it's emitted on the *first* successful one).

---

## How to apply this to your actual program

The pieces you'd lift, in dependency order:

1. **`load_user_module` + page-table setup** — mostly reusable as-is. Swap the bounded `user_image_pages[16]` for a real allocator when your modules exceed 16 pages, and map more than one stack page.
2. **`minemu_enter_user`** — reusable verbatim; just pass your real entry and stack top.
3. **The trampoline `svc.S`** — reusable verbatim as long as `minemu_trap_frame` stays 88 bytes. It's already offset-checked by `trap.h`'s static asserts.
4. **`minemu_svc_dispatch`** — this is where your real design goes. Replace the single hardcoded `UART_PUTCHAR` with a dispatch table (the ABI header `hello_syscall.h` shows the pattern: shared `#define`s both sides include). Your README note says Assignment 2 swaps this for the required `ioctl` interface.
5. **User side** — `syscall.S` generalizes cleanly: keep the `r7` = number / `r0` = arg convention and add a real libc-style wrapper.

The one structural thing to internalize: **there's no separate kernel/user address-space switch.** You install the user's pages into the low region of the *live* directory, and privilege is changed only by `movs pc, lr` (enter) and `movs pc, lr` (return from trap). Everything else is just building and unbuilding that 88-byte frame.

Here's my read on the changes. The good news: the example already contains 90% of what you need — the loader tracks per-page vaddrs and flags (`user_page_vaddrs[]` / `user_page_flags[]`), and the user page table is installed in the *live* kernel page directory, so the kernel can reach user memory directly. You mainly need to re-decode the frame's registers and add validation.

## 1. What you don't change

`kernel/svc.S` stays byte-for-byte identical — the frame layout is ABI (pinned by `trap.h`'s `_Static_assert`s) and the trampoline already gives you `r0-r3`, which is exactly the four ioctl arguments. Same for `minemu_enter_user` and the entry-mode checks at the top of the dispatcher.

Also note `MINEMU_SYSCALL_IOCTL` is `1`, and so was `MINEMU_HELLO_SYSCALL_UART_PUTCHAR` — `r7 == 1` means "ioctl" in both ABIs. You're not adding a branch alongside the old syscall; you're **reinterpreting the same r7==1** and dropping the byte-argument meaning entirely.

## 2. Rewrite the dispatch body to decode r0–r3

The current code treats `r0` as the byte to print:

```c
if (instruction != A32_SVC_ZERO || frame->r[7] != MINEMU_HELLO_SYSCALL_UART_PUTCHAR ||
    frame->r[0] > UINT8_MAX) { ... }
MINEMU_UART0->tx_data = frame->r[0];
```

That whole tail gets replaced. Per `user/lib/src/ioctl.c`, the user stub puts **fd in r0, request in r1, arg0 in r2, arg1 in r3**:

```c
#include "minemu/user_abi.h"      /* replaces ../include/hello_syscall.h */

struct minemu_trap_frame *minemu_svc_dispatch(struct minemu_trap_frame *frame) {
    uint32_t mode = frame->spsr & CPSR_MODE_MASK;
    if (frame->exception_id != MINEMU_EXCEPTION_SVC || mode != CPSR_MODE_USR ||
        (frame->spsr & CPSR_THUMB) != 0) {
        frame->r[0] = (uint32_t)MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
        return frame;
    }
    uint32_t instruction;
    if (!user_copy_from(&instruction, frame->fault_pc, sizeof(instruction)) ||
        instruction != A32_SVC_ZERO) {
        frame->r[0] = (uint32_t)MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
        return frame;
    }
    if (frame->r[7] != MINEMU_SYSCALL_IOCTL) {
        frame->r[0] = (uint32_t)MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
        return frame;
    }
    if (!user_syscall_observed) { /* keep your trace event */ }
    frame->r[0] = (uint32_t)ioctl_dispatch((int32_t)frame->r[0], frame->r[1],
                                           frame->r[2], frame->r[3]);
    return frame;
}
```

Two behavioural differences to be aware of: the mode/type/`svc #0` guards are unchanged in spirit, but **every failure now returns `MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR` (-1)** instead of the old `MINEMU_HELLO_SYSCALL_ERROR`. Signatures match `minemu/syscall.h`, so the trampoline needs no edits.

## 3. The one genuinely new thing: user-pointer validation

This is the change people miss. The old demo only ever dereferenced `frame->fault_pc` (always user `.text`) and a register value. Now `r2` for `UART_READ/WRITE` and `RNG_NEXT/STATE` is a **user virtual address the kernel must touch**, and a bad one currently takes a data abort → `minemu_abort_dispatch` → `minemu_fail_stop()` — user code crashing the kernel.

Add a translator mirroring `process-basics/kernel/address_space.c:369` (`kernel_pointer`), but reading the example's existing `user_page_table` directly:

```c
static void *user_pointer(uint32_t vaddr, uint32_t required) {
    /* must be inside the low user region: page-table index aliases otherwise */
    if (vaddr < USER_IMAGE_BASE || vaddr >= USER_STACK_TOP) return NULL;
    uint32_t pte = user_page_table[(vaddr >> 12) & 1023U];
    if ((pte & (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) !=
        (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) return NULL;
    uint32_t phys = pte & MINEMU_PTE_PAGE_MASK;
    return (void *)(uintptr_t)(MINEMU_KERNEL_DIRECT_BASE + phys - MINEMU_RAM_BASE
                               + (vaddr & (MINEMU_PAGE_SIZE - 1U)));
}
```

The `USER_IMAGE_BASE` bound matters: `(vaddr >> 12) & 1023` aliases, so `vaddr = 0` would falsely match the first text page. Don't omit it.

Two notes here:

- **The stack page works automatically** with this approach — it's already in `user_page_table` (the loader installs it separately from `user_page_index`, so a lookup based on `user_page_vaddrs[]` would *miss* it). That matters because `RNG_NEXT`'s out-pointer is typically a local like `uint32_t value` on the user stack (`tests/hw2/fixtures/devices/main.c:18`).
- Range checks must walk page-by-page with overflow detection, like `process-basics`' `range_has_flags`. I'd wrap it as `user_copy_from(dst, vaddr, len)` / `user_copy_to(vaddr, src, len)` so no call site ever dereferences a raw user address.
- `.text` pages are R+X but not W, so `RNG_STATE`/`UART_READ` into a `.rodata` address correctly fails — that's the point of passing `required` flags.

## 4. Add `ioctl_dispatch` — a straight port of the existing pattern

`examples/process-basics/kernel/syscall.c:61` is already a complete implementation of this exact contract; you're adapting it to the example's single-address-space world (no `process_current_space()` — there's one static `user_page_table`):

```c
static int32_t ioctl_dispatch(int32_t fd, uint32_t request,
                              uint32_t argument0, uint32_t argument1) {
    switch (request) {
    case MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_WRITE: {
        if (fd != MINEMU_FD_UART_OUT && fd != MINEMU_FD_UART_DIAG)
            return MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
        if (argument1 > MINEMU_IOCTL_MAX_TRANSFER) return MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
        uint8_t buffer[MINEMU_IOCTL_MAX_TRANSFER];
        if (!user_copy_from(buffer, argument0, argument1))
            return MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < argument1; ++i) {
            while ((MINEMU_UART0->status & MINEMU_UART_STATUS_TX_READY) == 0) { }
            MINEMU_UART0->tx_data = buffer[i];
        }
        return (int32_t)argument1;
    }
    case MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ:    /* fd must be MINEMU_FD_UART_IN; drain
                                       rx_data into buffer while RX_READY,
                                       then user_copy_to; return count */
    case MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_STATUS:  /* fd in {UART_IN, UART_OUT, UART_DIAG};
                                       return RX_READY|TX_READY bits */
    case MINEMU_IOCTL_RNG_NEXT:
    case MINEMU_IOCTL_RNG_STATE: {  /* fd == MINEMU_FD_RNG; value = RNG->data
                                       or RNG->state; user_copy_to(arg0,...);
                                       return 0 */ }
    case MINEMU_IOCTL_RNG_SEED:     /* fd == MINEMU_FD_RNG; RNG->seed = arg0 */
    case MINEMU_IOCTL_TRACE_EVENT:  /* fd == MINEMU_FD_TRACE;
                                       MINEMU_TRACE->event = arg0; return 0 */
    default:
        return MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
    }
}
```

Peripherals all come from `minemu/platform.h` — `MINEMU_UART0`, `MINEMU_RNG`, `MINEMU_TRACE` are already `#define`s there, with `struct` layouts and `MINEMU_UART_STATUS_*` bits, so you don't need the hand-rolled `struct example_uart_regs` that process-basics defines locally. The example already includes `minemu/platform.h`.

The discipline worth copying from process-basics: **check the fd before anything else** (`UART_IN` only reads, `UART_OUT/DIAG` only write, `RNG` only RNG, `TRACE` only trace) — that's what makes this an *access-control* mechanism rather than just a rename of the demo syscall.

## 5. User side

`user/syscall.S` (the hand-rolled `r7`/`svc #0` stub) becomes redundant — `user/lib/src/ioctl.c` already implements `ioctl()` with the correct register convention, and `user/Makefile` already links `libminimum_user.a` via `common.mk`. So:

- `user/main.c`: `#include "minemu/user_abi.h"` and replace the loop with
  `ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_OUT, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_WRITE, message, sizeof(message) - 1U);`
- Delete `user/syscall.S` (or keep it only if you want the example to show a bare-metal stub).
- `include/hello_syscall.h` can go away entirely, or shrink to just the `TRACE_USER_SYSCALL` constant you still emit internally.

## 6. Knock-on effects to keep in mind

- **`test.toml` still passes as written** — `uart0_contains = "hello world"` and `trace_values = [0x48454c10]` both hold if you keep the once-only `minemu_trace_event(TRACE_USER_SYSCALL)`. Keep that event gated exactly as it is: if you ever point this example's test at user-generated trace values (as `tests/hw2/devices.toml` does with `[0x4d454d55, ...]`), an unconditional internal trace event would corrupt the expected sequence.
- **The old `hello_syscall.h` error constant** (`-1`) and `MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR` (`-1`) coincide, so return-value semantics don't shift — but update any comparison in `user/main.c` accordingly.
- **`MAX_USER_IMAGE_PAGES 16`** is unchanged and fine; ioctl adds no kernel-side buffers beyond the 256-byte bounce array.

## Decision points I'd flag before you start

1. **Bounce buffer vs. direct access.** I sketched a 256-byte stack bounce buffer because that's what process-basics does and it keeps `MAX_TRANSFER` bounded. Since the kernel can address user memory directly here, you *could* validate the range and stream straight from user RAM to the UART — fewer copies, but the transfer is then only bounded by your validation loop. I'd match process-basics (bounce) since your real program will eventually have multiple address spaces where direct access isn't available.
2. **How far to go on validation.** The sketch validates every buffer pointer. static void *user_pointer(uint32_t vaddr, uint32_t required) {
    if (vaddr < USER_IMAGE_BASE || vaddr >= USER_STACK_TOP) {
        return NULL;
    }
    uint32_t pte = user_page_table[(vaddr >> 12) & 1023U];
    if ((pte & (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) !=
        (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) {
        return NULL;
    }
    uint32_t physical = pte & MINEMU_PTE_PAGE_MASK;
    return (void *)(uintptr_t)(MINEMU_KERNEL_DIRECT_BASE + physical -
                               MINEMU_RAM_BASE + (vaddr & (MINEMU_PAGE_SIZE - 1U)));
}
```

Note MINEMU_KERNEL_DIRECT_BASE = 0xc0000000, MINEMU_RAM_BASE = 0x40000000. kernel_vaddr_to_paddr does vaddr - DIRECT_BASE + RAM_BASE. So inverse: paddr + DIRECT_BASE - RAM_BASE. Yes matches.

Then range check:

```c
static bool user_range(uint32_t vaddr, uint32_t length, uint32_t required) {
    if (length == 0) return true;   /* or handle specially */
    if (vaddr < USER_IMAGE_BASE || vaddr > USER_STACK_TOP) return false;
    if (length > USER_STACK_TOP - vaddr) return false;   /* overflow-safe */
    for (uint32_t page = vaddr & MINEMU_PTE_PAGE_MASK;
         page < vaddr + length; page += MINEMU_PAGE_SIZE) {
        uint32_t pte = user_page_table[(page >> 12) & 1023U];
        if ((pte & (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) !=
            (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

static bool user_range_readable(uint32_t vaddr, uint32_t length) {
    return user_range(vaddr, length, MINEMU_PTE_READABLE);
}
static bool user_range_writable(uint32_t vaddr, uint32_t length) {
    return user_range(vaddr, length, MINEMU_PTE_WRITABLE);
}
static bool user_copy_from(void *destination, uint32_t source, uint32_t length) {
    const uint8_t *in = ...; walk page by page;
}
```

I went through your `main.c` against the kernel's actual build system, startup assembly, and the hw2 test fixtures. The user-mode *logic* you copied from the example is mostly right — but four things stop it from working, and two are silent failures that compile fine and just hang.

## 1. It won't link: `svc.S` and `user.S` aren't in the Makefile

This is the big one. `kernel/Makefile:11-19` builds this object list:

```make
RUNTIME_OBJECTS := \
	$(BUILD)/runtime/block.o \
	$(BUILD)/runtime/exception.o \
	$(BUILD)/runtime/memory.o \
	$(BUILD)/runtime/trace.o \
	$(BUILD)/startup/boot.o \
	$(BUILD)/startup/vectors.o \
	$(BUILD)/runtime/uart.o \
	$(BUILD)/runtime/cprintf.o
```

`startup/svc.o` and `startup/user.o` are absent. I confirmed against the build dir — only `boot.o`, `vectors.o`, `irq.o` exist under `startup/` — and `nm` on the built ELF shows:

```
c0030674 W minemu_svc_trampoline
```

**`W` = weak.** That's the stub in `kernel/src/runtime/exception.c:15`:

```c
__attribute__((weak, noreturn)) void minemu_svc_trampoline(void) {
    minemu_fail_stop();
}
```

So two failures:

- `minemu_enter_user` is declared (`main.c:43`) and called (`main.c:432`) but **defined nowhere** → hard undefined-reference link error.
- Even after you link `svc.o`, the **weak stub wins and the first `svc #0` spins forever in `minemu_fail_stop()`** — no error, no output, just a hang. This is the trap: the ELF links, boots, enters user mode, and dies on the first syscall.

And there's a subtlety in how you fix it. Don't just add them to `RUNTIME_OBJECTS` — that puts them in `libminemu_kernel.a`, where archive extraction order decides the winner. `exception.o` sits *before* `vectors.o` in the archive, so it gets pulled in first (for `minemu_fail_stop`), defines the weak `minemu_svc_trampoline`, and by the time `vectors.o` references the symbol it's already satisfied — `svc.o` is never extracted, weak stub persists.

Mirror what the Makefile already does for IRQ. Note `IRQ_OBJECT` is deliberately kept *out* of the archive:

```make
IRQ_OBJECT := $(BUILD)/startup/irq.o
...
OBJECTS := $(CORE_OBJECT) $(IRQ_OBJECT) $(RUNTIME_OBJECTS)
```

Do the same:

```make
SVC_OBJECT  := $(BUILD)/startup/svc.o
USER_OBJECT := $(BUILD)/startup/user.o
OBJECTS := $(CORE_OBJECT) $(IRQ_OBJECT) $(SVC_OBJECT) $(USER_OBJECT) $(RUNTIME_OBJECTS)
...
$(KERNEL): $(CORE_OBJECT) $(IRQ_OBJECT) $(SVC_OBJECT) $(USER_OBJECT) $(RUNTIME) linker/kernel.ld
	$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) $(CORE_OBJECT) $(IRQ_OBJECT) $(SVC_OBJECT) $(USER_OBJECT) $(RUNTIME) $(LIBGCC) -o $@
```

Direct objects are already in the link before the archive gets scanned, so their strong definitions beat the weak ones.

## 2. It won't compile: four helpers are called but never defined

`user_copy_from`, `user_copy_to`, `user_range_readable`, `user_range_writable` are used at `main.c:320, 342, 362, 366, 369, 395` but exist nowhere in the repo — I grepped every header under `kernel/include` and all sources. With `-std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror` those are immediate errors.

You need to add them. The critical design point I flagged last time is now confirmed concrete: **walk `user_page_table` directly, not `user_page_vaddrs[]`.** Your loader installs the stack page separately from the image pages:

```c
user_page_table[(USER_STACK_BOTTOM >> 12) & 1023U] =
    kernel_vaddr_to_paddr(user_stack) | MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | ...
```

It never touches `user_page_vaddrs[]` / `user_page_count`. And the `RNG_STATE`/`RNG_NEXT` out-pointer in `tests/hw2/fixtures/devices/main.c:18` is `uint32_t value` — **a stack local.** A helper that scans the page list would reject it and the devices test would fail.

Shape that works for both:

```c
static void *user_pointer(uint32_t vaddr, uint32_t required) {
    if (vaddr < USER_IMAGE_BASE || vaddr >= USER_STACK_TOP) {
        return NULL;                        /* (vaddr>>12)&1023 aliases; must bound it */
    }
    uint32_t pte = user_page_table[(vaddr >> 12) & 1023U];
    if ((pte & (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) !=
        (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) {
        return NULL;
    }
    uint32_t physical = pte & MINEMU_PTE_PAGE_MASK;
    return (void *)(uintptr_t)(MINEMU_KERNEL_DIRECT_BASE + physical -
                               MINEMU_RAM_BASE + (vaddr & (MINEMU_PAGE_SIZE - 1U)));
}
```

Then `user_range_readable/writable` walk page-by-page with overflow-safe bounds (`length > USER_STACK_TOP - vaddr` after checking `vaddr <= USER_STACK_TOP`), and the two copy helpers loop calling `user_pointer` per chunk. The stack page is reached automatically because it's in the table.

## 3. `RNG_SEED` has three separate bugs (`main.c:368-373`)

```c
case MINEMU_IOCTL_RNG_SEED: {
    if (fd != MINEMU_FD_RNG || !user_range_readable(argument0, sizeof(uint32_t))) {
        return MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
    }
    MINEMU_RNG->state = argument0;
}                                              // ← no return!
case MINEMU_IOCTL_TRACE_EVENT: {
```

- **No `return`** → falls through into `TRACE_EVENT`, where `fd == MINEMU_FD_RNG != MINEMU_FD_TRACE`, so seeding always returns -1. It's also a **compile error**: `-Wimplicit-fallthrough` is on via `-Wextra`, and `-Werror` makes it fatal.
- **`user_range_readable` on `argument0` is wrong.** Per `user/lib/src/ioctl.c:37`, `RNG_SEED`'s argument0 is the seed *value*, not a pointer. The devices fixture calls `ioctl(MINEMU_FD_RNG, MINEMU_IOCTL_RNG_SEED, UINT32_C(0x12345678))` — `0x12345678` is outside your user range, so the check rejects it.
- **Writes `->state` instead of `->seed`.** The register layout in `minemu/platform.h:105` is `{seed, data, state}`, and `examples/process-basics/kernel/syscall.c:105` does `RNG->seed = argument0;`.

That matters for the assertion in `tests/hw2/devices.toml:10`:

```toml
trace_values = [0x4d454d55, 0x791c7b62, 0x12345678, 0x87985aa5]
```

`0x4d454d55` is `MINEMU_RNG_DEFAULT_SEED` and `0x12345678` is the value seeded mid-test — so the seed must actually reach the seed register for that sequence to come out right. Correct form:

```c
case MINEMU_IOCTL_RNG_SEED:
    if (fd != MINEMU_FD_RNG) {
        return MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR;
    }
    MINEMU_RNG->seed = argument0;
    return 0;
```

## 4. Wrong module name: `"user-hello"` vs `"minimum-user"`

`main.c:410` searches for `"user-hello"`, but that string belongs to the *example*'s own manifest (`examples/user-mode-hello/image.toml:4`). Your real packaging uses `"minimum-user"`:

- `image/minimum.toml:4` — `name = "minimum-user"`
- `tests/hw2/fixtures/hello/image.toml:4` — `name = "minimum-user"`
- `tests/hw2/fixtures/devices/image.toml:4` — `name = "minimum-user"`

`find_module` returns NULL → trace `0xb007bad1` → `minemu_fail_stop()`. Every hw2 test dies at boot before entering user mode. Change the literal to `"minimum-user"` (or better, a `static const char module_name[]` like the example uses).

---

## One design conflict you should decide on before proceeding

You commented out the shell and replaced it with `minemu_enter_user`, which is `noreturn`. But `tests/hw2/msh-*.toml` (four tests: prompt, echo, editing, overlong) boot `image/build/minimum.img` and assert `"msh> "` output. With the shell commented out, those four fail.

The kernel ELF is shared across all of these, so you can't have one image enter user mode and another run the shell from the same boot path — unless the shell itself moves into the user program. `user/prog/minimum-user/main.c` is currently a bare `nop` loop, which is the untouched starter. The coherent reading is: **hw2 wants the shell rewritten as a user-mode program**, with `ioctl` as its device interface — which also explains why `hello.toml` and `devices.toml` assert `cpu_mode = "user"` while the msh tests assert nothing about mode.

Worth confirming against your assignment spec before you build on either interpretation, because it changes whether the shell block stays in the kernel (temporarily) or gets ported to `user/prog/minimum-user/`.

## Also worth noting

- `uart_init()` is only called inside the commented-out shell block (`main.c:452`). It sets `MINEMU_UART_CONTROL_RX_IRQ_ENABLE`. Your `ioctl` UART paths poll `status` and don't need RX interrupts, so `UART_WRITE`/`UART_READ` work without it — but if you keep any interrupt-driven input path, it must be called before user mode, since `minemu_enter_user` does `cpsid if` and nothing re-enables IRQs afterward.
- Your `minemu_irq_dispatch` is fine and correctly overrides the weak one, but it's now unreachable dead code once you enter user mode and never return.
- `main.c` uses `uint32_t`/`UINT32_C` without `#include <stdint.h>` — it gets them transitively via `minemu/boot.h`. Works, but fragile; adding the include costs nothing.

---

**Suggested order:** Makefile objects first (that's the link error + the silent hang), then the four helpers, then module name, then `RNG_SEED`. After step 2 you should be able to get `hello.toml` passing — that test only exercises `UART_WRITE` from a `.data` buffer, so it needs no stack access and is the cheapest end-to-end confirmation that user mode + the SVC round trip work. Then `devices.toml`, which is the one that actually stresses the stack-pointer and seed-register cases.

Partially — 3 of the 4 issues are fixed, but 2 remain, and one of them is the exact stack-page bug I flagged.

## Fixed ✅

**Makefile** — `kernel/Makefile:11-12,23,65-67` are now correct. `svc.o` and `user.o` are direct objects on the link line, ahead of the archive, so their strong definitions beat the weak stubs in `exception.c`. This was the silent-hang bug; it's properly resolved.

**`RNG_SEED`** — `main.c:412-418` now does the right thing: fd check, `MINEMU_RNG->seed = argument0`, `return 0`. No fallthrough, no bogus pointer validation. The `-Wimplicit-fallthrough` compile error is gone.

**Helpers exist** — `user_range_readable/writable`, `user_copy_from/to` are defined and wired into all the call sites.

## Still broken ❌

**1. Module name — `main.c:472` still says `"user-hello"`**

```c
find_module(boot_info, "user-hello", sizeof("user-hello") - 1U);
```

Every hw2 image packages the module as `"minimum-user"`:
- `image/minimum.toml:4`
- `tests/hw2/fixtures/hello/image.toml:4`
- `tests/hw2/fixtures/devices/image.toml:4`

So `find_module` returns NULL → trace `0xb007bad1` → `minemu_fail_stop()`. **This kills all hw2 tests at boot**, including the two user-mode ones. Change the literal to `"minimum-user"`.

**2. The helpers walk the wrong table — stack page is invisible**

This is the one I warned about, and it's there:

```c
static bool user_range_writable(uint32_t vaddr, size_t length) {
    ...
    int index = user_page_index(page, 0, false);   /* walks user_page_vaddrs[] */
```

But your loader installs the stack page directly into the table, bypassing that array:

```c
user_page_table[(USER_STACK_BOTTOM >> 12) & 1023U] =
    kernel_vaddr_to_paddr(user_stack) | MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | ...;
```

`user_page_vaddrs[]` only ever contains image pages (`prepare_user_range` is called solely for segments, which are bounded above by `USER_STACK_BOTTOM = 0x007ff000`), so `0x007ff000` is never in it. `user_page_index` returns −1 → `user_range_writable` returns false.

In `tests/hw2/fixtures/devices/main.c:18`, `uint32_t value` is the RNG out-pointer, and `&value` is taken, so it must live in memory — on the user stack. **`devices.toml` will fail at the first `RNG_STATE` call** with `MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR`.

Note `hello.toml` still passes this check: its buffer is `static char message[]` in `.data`, an image page with `WRITABLE`. So you'd see hello succeed and devices fail, which is a confusing signal unless you know why.

Two smaller defects in the same functions:
- **No bounds check on `vaddr` at all.** `end = vaddr + length` can wrap; if `end` wraps below `page`, the loop body never runs and the function returns `true` for an arbitrary address. Add the `vaddr < USER_IMAGE_BASE || vaddr >= USER_STACK_TOP` guard (and note `(vaddr >> 12) & 1023` aliases, so without the guard a low address matches a legit high page).
- `length == 0` returns true without validating `vaddr`. Minor, but `UART_READ` with count 0 exploits it harmlessly today.

The fix is to stop going through `user_page_index` and read `user_page_table` directly, which reaches image and stack pages uniformly:

```c
static bool user_range(uint32_t vaddr, size_t length, uint32_t required) {
    if (length == 0) {
        return vaddr >= USER_IMAGE_BASE && vaddr <= USER_STACK_TOP;
    }
    if (vaddr < USER_IMAGE_BASE || vaddr > USER_STACK_TOP ||
        length > USER_STACK_TOP - vaddr) {
        return false;
    }
    uint32_t end = vaddr + length;
    for (uint32_t page = vaddr & MINEMU_PTE_PAGE_MASK; page < end;
         page += MINEMU_PAGE_SIZE) {
        uint32_t pte = user_page_table[(page >> 12) & 1023U];
        if ((pte & (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) !=
            (MINEMU_PTE_VALID | MINEMU_PTE_USER | required)) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}
```

(`required` = `MINEMU_PTE_READABLE` or `MINEMU_PTE_WRITABLE`; the two existing functions become one-line wrappers.)

One thing I'd leave as-is: `user_copy_from/to` dereference the user VA directly (`(uint8_t *)(uintptr_t)user_src`). That's actually correct here — the user page table is installed in the live page directory (`main.c:304`), and privileged accesses ignore `PTE_USER`. No need to translate through the direct map.

## Diagnosis

Decode those numbers:

| Test | Value |
|---|---|
| expected | `0x4d454d55`, `0x791c7b62`, `0x12345678`, `0x87985aa5` |
| got | **`0x48454c10`**, `0x4d454d55`, `0x791c7b62`, `0x12345678`, `0x87985aa5` |

`1212501008` = `0x48454c10` = `TRACE_USER_SYSCALL`. Your sequence is otherwise *exactly* right — the kernel just prepends one extra event.

That's the leftover from the example, at `kernel/src/core/main.c:450-453`:

```c
if (!user_syscall_observed) {
    minemu_trace_event(TRACE_USER_SYSCALL);
    user_syscall_observed = true;
}
```

It's demo instrumentation from `examples/user-mode-hello`, where it exists so that example's own `test.toml` can assert `trace_values = [0x48454c10]` as proof user code ran a syscall. In the canonical kernel it has no such job — and because `tests/hw2/devices.toml` asserts the trace array *exactly*, the extra event corrupts it.

`hello.toml` passed only because it has no `trace_values` assertion; the same extra event was emitted there and simply went unchecked.

## What this confirms about your fixes

All four device values landing in order means the rest is genuinely working:

- **Stack page reachable** — `RNG_STATE`/`RNG_NEXT` write to `uint32_t value`, a user stack local. Those succeeded, so your `user_range_*` rewrite correctly consults `user_page_table` rather than `user_page_vaddrs[]`. That was the bug I'd flagged; it's resolved.
- **`RNG_SEED` fixed** — `0x12345678` appears as the third value (seed read back as state), and the fourth value `0x87985aa5` is correctly derived *from* that seed. Wrong register or missing `return` would have produced `MINEMU_IOCTL_ERROR` or a stale state here.
- **Module name fixed** — it booted and reached user mode at all, so `find_module` found `"minimum-user"`.
- **SVC round trip fixed** — no hang, so `svc.o`/`user.o` are winning over the weak stubs.

## The fix

Delete the block at `main.c:450-453`, and then clean up the two things it leaves orphaned:

- `static bool user_syscall_observed;` (`main.c:34`) — becomes unused. GCC's `-Wunused-variable` fires on unused file-scope statics, and you build with `-Werror`, so leaving it is a compile error, not just dead code.
- `#define TRACE_USER_SYSCALL UINT32_C(0x48454c10)` (`main.c:23`) — unused macro, harmless (no warning), but worth removing for tidiness.

Leave `examples/user-mode-hello/kernel/main.c` alone — it's a separate tree with its own copy, and its test depends on the event.

#include <stdint.h>
#include "minemu/user_abi.h"

#define MAX_LINE_LENGTH 20

static char buffer[MAX_LINE_LENGTH + 1];
static uint32_t buffer_index;

static void write_string(const char *text) {
    uint32_t length = 0;
    while (text[length] != '\0') {
        ++length;
    }
    (void)ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_OUT, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_WRITE,
                (void *)(uintptr_t)text, length);
}

static int32_t read_some(uint8_t *bytes, uint32_t capacity) {
    return ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ, bytes, capacity);
}

/* Ports the ISR body verbatim; only the byte source moved to ioctl. */
static bool consume(uint8_t c) {
    if (c == '\n') {
        return true;
    }
    if (c == 0x08 || c == 0x7f) {
        if (buffer_index > 0) {
            --buffer_index;
        }
    } else if (buffer_index < MAX_LINE_LENGTH) {
        buffer[buffer_index++] = (char)c;
    }
    return false;
}

static bool read_line(void) {
    uint8_t chunk[16];
    for (;;) {
        int32_t count = read_some(chunk, sizeof(chunk));
        if (count < 0) {
            return false;
        }
        for (int32_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
            if (consume(chunk[i])) {
                buffer[buffer_index] = '\0';
                return true;
            }
        }
    }
}

void minemu_user_main(void) {
    for (;;) {
        write_string("msh> ");
        if (!read_line()) {
            for (;;) { }
        }
        char *ptr = buffer;
        while (*ptr == ' ') ++ptr;
        if (*ptr == '\0') continue;
        if (memcmp(ptr, "echo", 4) == 0 && (ptr[4] == ' ' || ptr[4] == '\0')) {
            char *arg = ptr + 4;
            while (*arg == ' ') ++arg;
            write_string(arg);
            write_string("\n");
        } else {
            char *start = ptr;
            char *end = ptr;
            while (*end != ' ' && *end != '\0') ++end;
            *end = '\0';
            write_string("command not found: ");
            write_string(start);
            write_string("\n");
        }
    }
}
```

The answer structure:

1. **The ISR model doesn't exist in user mode.** Three reasons:
   - `minemu_enter_user` does `cpsid if` → IRQs masked
   - USR mode cannot write CPSR I/F bits (privileged)

   - `MINEMU_UART0->status & RX_READY` → `ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_STATUS, ...) & MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_RX_READY`
   - `MINEMU_UART0->rx_data` → `ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ, &c, 1)`
   
   The line-assembly state machine (backspace, buffer_index, newline, MAX_LINE_LENGTH) is pure logic — it ports as-is, but the shared globals become locals because there's no ISR to race with.

Let me write the actual code.

```c
#include <stdint.h>
#include "minemu/user_abi.h"
#include "string.h"

#define MAX_LINE_LENGTH 20

static char buffer[MAX_LINE_LENGTH + 1];
static size_t buffer_index;

/* Returns true when a complete line is in `buffer`. */
static bool read_line(void) {
    for (;;) {
        uint8_t c;
        if (ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ, &c, 1) != 1) {
            continue; /* nothing buffered yet */
        }
        if (c == '\n') {
            buffer[buffer_index] = '\0';
            return true;
        }
        if (c == 0x08 || c == 0x7f) {
            if (buffer_index > 0) {
                --buffer_index;
            }
        } else if (buffer_index < MAX_LINE_LENGTH) {
            buffer[buffer_index++] = (char)c;
        }
    }
}
```

Wait — there's a subtlety. The original ISR drained the whole FIFO per interrupt and set `newline = true` when it saw '\n', but kept draining remaining bytes after. In the polling version, we return as soon as we see '\n', leaving any subsequent bytes in the FIFO for the next `read_line()` call. That's actually *better* — it preserves the split correctly. Good.

But there's a bug risk: if the input arrives as "cmd1\ncmd2\n" in one burst, the ISR version would set newline=true on the first \n and *continue* draining, putting "cmd2" chars into the buffer too — a pre-existing bug in the ISR version (it doesn't stop at newline). The polling version fixes that naturally. Worth mentioning.

    for (;;) {

        read_line();

        char *ptr = buffer;
        while (*ptr == ' ') ++ptr;
        if (*ptr == '\0') continue;

        if (memcmp(ptr, "echo", 4) == 0 && (ptr[4] == ' ' || ptr[4] == '\0')) {

            write_string("command not found: ");

            write_string("\n");

    }
}
```

Let me focus on the real technical answer:

**Core point: the UART handler cannot be ported as an interrupt handler.** Reasons:
1. `minemu_enter_user` does `cpsid if` — IRQs and FIQs masked in user mode. And USR mode cannot change CPSR I/F bits (privileged only). So no interrupts will ever be delivered while in user mode.
2. The MMIO window is mapped supervisor-only: boot.S:88 writes `0x10000013` — flags 0x13 = VALID|WRITABLE|READABLE|EXECUTABLE but **no PTE_USER (4)**. So `MINEMU_UART0->status` from USR mode = data abort → `minemu_abort_dispatch` → fail_stop. User code physically cannot touch the UART registers.

So the handler's *job* (assemble a line from bytes, handle backspace, detect newline) must move into user space as a **polled** loop using the ioctl ABI that already exists in your kernel:
- `ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_STATUS, ...)` → returns RX_READY/TX_READY bits
- `ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ, buf, n)` → reads up to n bytes, returns count
- `ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_OUT, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_WRITE, buf, n)` → writes

That's exactly the shape of the ports: ISR-driven → poll-driven. The line-editing state machine (buffer, buffer_index, backspace handling, newline) ports verbatim — it's pure logic, no hardware.

Concretely in user/prog/minimum-user/main.c:

```c
#include <stdint.h>
#include "minemu/user_abi.h"

#define MAX_LINE_LENGTH 20

static char buffer[MAX_LINE_LENGTH + 1];
static uint32_t buffer_index;

static void write_string(const char *s) {
    uint32_t len = 0;
    while (s[len]) ++len;
    ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_OUT, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_WRITE, (void *)s, len);
}

static void read_line(void) {
    for (;;) {
        uint8_t c;
        /* poll: one byte at a time */
        while ((ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_STATUS, 0, 0)
                & MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_RX_READY) == 0) { }
        if (ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ, &c, 1) != 1)
            continue;
        if (c == '\n') { buffer[buffer_index] = '\0'; return; }
        if (c == 0x08 || c == 0x7f) { if (buffer_index) --buffer_index; }
        else if (buffer_index < MAX_LINE_LENGTH) buffer[buffer_index++] = (char)c;
    }
}
```

Wait — careful with `MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ` semantics in *your* kernel: it drains while RX_READY and returns count. If nothing is ready it returns 0. So polling STATUS first then READ(1) works. Or simply loop READ(&c,1) until it returns 1 — simpler, no STATUS needed. That's cleaner.

for (;;) {
    uint8_t c;
    if (ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ, &c, 1) == 1) { ... process ... }
}
```

Now I have what I need. There are two hard constraints that decide the design, both visible in `boot.S`.

## You can't port it as an interrupt handler

The original `uart_handler` was an ISR — the UART raised IRQ 1, `minemu_irq_dispatch` called it, it drained the RX FIFO. Two things make that impossible in user mode:

**1. User mode can never take interrupts.** `minemu_enter_user` (`user.S:10`) starts with `cpsid if`. The I/F bits in CPSR are privileged — USR mode cannot write them. So once you enter user mode, interrupts are masked *forever*. `minemu_irq_enable()` won't help; it's an `msr` that faults or is ignored from USR.

**2. User mode can't touch the UART registers at all.** The bootstrap maps the MMIO window supervisor-only. `boot.S:88`:

```asm
ldr r1, =0x10000013      @ VALID(1) | WRITABLE(2) | EXECUTABLE(8) | READABLE(16)
```

`0x13` has no `PTE_USER` bit (`4`). Your loader is careful to set `MINEMU_PTE_USER` on user pages (`main.c:296, 300`); the MMIO identity map deliberately doesn't. So `MINEMU_UART0->status` from USR mode is a permission fault → `minemu_data_abort_entry` → `minemu_abort_dispatch` → `minemu_fail_stop()`. Hard hang, no output.

So: **all device access must go through the ioctl layer you already built.** That's not a workaround, it's the architecture the MMU permissions are enforcing.

## What actually moves

The handler has two parts, and only one of them is hardware:

- **Byte source** — `MINEMU_UART0->status & RX_READY` / `MINEMU_UART0->rx_data` → replaced by `ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ, ...)`.
- **Line-editing state machine** — backspace, buffer cap, newline detection, the "is this line empty" check. This is pure logic with no hardware dependency. **It ports verbatim.**

The shape changes from *interrupt-driven* to *polled*, because there's no way to block: your `minemu_svc_dispatch` only implements `MINEMU_SYSCALL_IOCTL` and returns `-1` for every other `r7`, so `sched_yield()` (declared in `user_abi.h:53`) just errors out. Busy-poll is the only option. Note your `UART_READ` is already non-blocking by design — it drains while `RX_READY` and returns the count, which is exactly what a poll loop wants.

## Where it goes

`user/prog/minimum-user/main.c` — that's what `image/minimum.toml:4-5` packages as `"minimum-user"`, and the three msh tests all boot `image/build/minimum.img`. The hw2 hello/devices fixtures package *different* ELFs under the same module name, so your kernel's `find_module(..., "minimum-user")` keeps working unchanged for all of them.

Sketch:

```c
#include <stdint.h>
#include "minemu/user_abi.h"

#define MAX_LINE_LENGTH 20

static char buffer[MAX_LINE_LENGTH + 1];
static uint32_t buffer_index;
static bool overflow;          /* see finding #2 below */

static void write_string(const char *text) {
    uint32_t length = 0;
    while (text[length] != '\0') { ++length; }
    (void)ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_OUT, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_WRITE,
                (void *)(uintptr_t)text, length);
}

/* Returns with a NUL-terminated line in buffer[]. */
static void read_line(void) {
    buffer_index = 0;
    overflow = false;
    for (;;) {
        uint8_t c;
        if (ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_IN, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_READ, &c, 1) != 1) {
            continue;                     /* nothing queued; poll again */
        }
        if (c == '\n') {
            buffer[buffer_index] = '\0';
            return;
        }
        if (c == 0x08 || c == 0x7f) {
            if (buffer_index > 0) { --buffer_index; }
        } else if (buffer_index < MAX_LINE_LENGTH) {
            buffer[buffer_index++] = (char)c;
        } else {
            overflow = true;
        }
    }
}
```

then `minemu_user_main` becomes your old shell body with `cprintf(...)` → `write_string(...)` and `while (!newline) {}` → `read_line()`.

Three consequences worth noting, since they're simplifications rather than costs:

- **`volatile` goes away.** `newline` needed it because the ISR and the main loop raced on it.
- **The critical sections go away.** `minemu_irq_disable()` / `minemu_irq_enable()` around the `memcpy` were protecting against the ISR mutating `buffer_index` mid-copy. With polling there's no ISR; `read_line` returns only when the line is complete, so there's nothing to race with.
- **`newline` itself disappears** — `read_line` returning *is* the newline signal.

You need `write_string` because the user lib has no printf. `user/lib/src/` contains only `process.c`, `memory.c`, `ioctl.c` — no `cprintf` equivalent, and the kernel's `cprintf.h` isn't in the user include path (`common.mk:18` sets `-I` to `user/lib/include` and `kernel/include`, and `cprintf.h` is kernel-only in spirit).

## Two test failures the old kernel shell would have had

Since you're rewriting this anyway, worth knowing the commented-out version doesn't satisfy the msh assertions as-is.

**1. `msh-overlong` requires dropping the line, not truncating it.** It asserts `uart0_contains = "msh> msh> "` — two *adjacent* prompts with nothing between. Your old code truncated at 20 and kept going, which emits `command not found: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\n` between them, destroying the adjacency. An overlong line has to produce no output at all. That's the `overflow` flag in the sketch: on `'\n'`, if `overflow`, clear and `continue` without processing. (Design call: whether backspacing out of overflow revives the line. Simplest is "once poisoned, always poisoned" — the test only needs that.)

**2. `msh-editing` expects whitespace normalization.** Input is `echx\bo   worked   fine  `; backspace removes the `x`, giving `echo   worked   fine`. But the expected output is `worked fine` — **single** space. Your echo path (`arg = ptr + 4; while (*arg == ' ') ++arg; cprintf("%s\n", arg)`) only strips *leading* spaces and would emit `worked   fine`.

I can't tell from the repo which side does the collapsing, because `uart0_contains` is implemented inside the `minemu` binary, which isn't source-available here. Two possibilities: the harness normalizes whitespace runs in both the expected and actual strings, or your shell is expected to tokenize on whitespace and rejoin with single spaces. **Worth a two-minute experiment**: make the shell emit `worked   fine`, run `just test hw2 editing`, and see whether it passes. If it does, the harness normalizes and you're done. If it fails, your echo needs to rebuild the argument from tokens. Don't guess this one — it's cheap to settle empirically.

## What to delete from the kernel

Once the shell lives in user space, these are dead:

- `static volatile bool newline` (`main.c:39`) — I checked: GCC does **not** warn on an unused `static volatile`, so `-Werror` won't catch it. It'll just sit there. Delete it manually.
- The commented-out `uart_handler` and shell block (`main.c:43-64`, `464-502`).
- `MAX_LINE_LENGTH` (`main.c:15`).
- In `minemu_irq_dispatch`, the UART branch is already commented out — leave it commented, or remove it. SYSTICK and BLOCK acks stay.

Do **not** delete `uart_init()` from `runtime/uart.c` — it's part of the supplied runtime library (`libminemu_kernel.a`), and nothing forces you to call it. You just stop calling it. Enabling `MINEMU_IRQ_UART0` in the interrupt controller is likewise unnecessary now that no one consumes RX interrupts.

## One risk to watch

`user/common/user.ld:10` puts `.bss` in a `NOLOAD` section, so `static char buffer[21]` adds a zero-filled page to your image. Your loader handles that correctly — `write_user_range(..., NULL, memory_size)` zero-fills, then `file_size` bytes are copied over. But it *does* add a page, and if `.bss` lands in the same page as a differently-flagged section, `user_page_index` returns `-1` on the flag mismatch and the load fails.

The failure signature is specific: trace `0xb007bad1` and `minemu_fail_stop()`. The hw2-hello fixture also has a static (`.data`) and loads fine, so the sections are evidently landing far enough apart today — but that was with a smaller program. If the shell image won't load, that's the first thing to check: disassemble `user/prog/minimum-user/build/minimum-user.elf` and look at the section-to-page layout. Making `buffer` a local in `read_line` instead of a file-scope static sidesteps it entirely if it bites.

## The actual bug

`image/minimum.toml:4-5`:

```toml
[[modules]]
name = "minimum-user"
elf = "../user/prog/minimum-user/build/minimum-user.elf"   ← still the nop loop
```

And `user/prog/minimum-user/main.c` is still:

```c
void minemu_user_main(void) {
    for (;;) { __asm__ volatile("nop"); }
}
```

So `minimum.img` contains kernel + silent nop loop. Your kernel boots, `find_module(..., "minimum-user")` succeeds, it enters user mode, and the program spins printing nothing forever. Hence `UART0 output did not contain expected text` — no prompt, no crash, no error.

The `Nothing to be done for 'all'` lines confirm it: the image is up to date w.r.t. `minimum.toml` + kernel + `minimum-user.elf`. `msh.elf` is never referenced by anything in the image path.

## Fix 1 — point the image at your shell

`image/minimum.toml`:

```toml
kernel = "../kernel/build/minimum-kernel.elf"

[[modules]]
name = "minimum-user"
elf = "../user/prog/msh/build/msh.elf"
```

**Keep the name `"minimum-user"`.** Don't rename it to `"msh"`. The kernel ELF is shared with the hw2 hello/devices fixtures, and both of those package their own program under the name `"minimum-user"`:

- `tests/hw2/fixtures/hello/image.toml:4` — `name = "minimum-user"`
- `tests/hw2/fixtures/devices/image.toml:4` — `name = "minimum-user"`

Your kernel searches for exactly one name (`main.c:444`). If you change that to `"msh"`, hello and devices break, because they'd still be packaged as `"minimum-user"`. Renaming the *ELF path* while keeping the *module name* is what lets all three groups coexist off one kernel.

## Fix 2 — teach the image Makefile about msh

`image/Makefile:5,14-21,30-31` only track `minimum-user`. So after Fix 1, editing `msh/main.c` would silently not rebuild the image — you'd be debugging stale bytes, which is a miserable way to spend an afternoon.

```make
USER_PROGRAM := ../user/prog/msh/build/msh.elf

USER_INPUTS := $(wildcard ../user/prog/msh/*.c) \
	$(wildcard ../user/prog/msh/*.S) \
	$(wildcard ../user/lib/src/*.c) \
	$(wildcard ../user/lib/include/*.h) \
	../user/common/common.mk \
	../user/common/user.ld \
	../user/lib/Makefile \
	../user/prog/msh/Makefile

$(USER_PROGRAM): $(USER_INPUTS)
	$(MAKE) -C ../user/prog/msh all
```

(`image/minimum.toml` is already a prerequisite of `$(IMAGE)` at line 33, so Fix 1 triggers a rebuild on its own.)

## Your msh code is otherwise sound

I checked the ELF — it's fine, and it clears the `.bss`-page risk I flagged last time. `readelf -lW`:

```
LOAD  0x001000 0x00400000 0x00400000 0x003d0 0x003ec RWE 0x1000
      Segment Sections...  00  .text .rodata .bss
```

`.text`, `.rodata`, `.bss` all sit in **one** `RWE` segment, one page. There's no mixed-flags page conflict, so `user_page_index` never returns −1 on a flag mismatch. `.bss` is NOBITS inside that segment (`FileSiz 0x3d0`, `MemSiz 0x3ec`), which your loader handles: `write_user_range(..., NULL, memory_size)` zero-fills, then `file_size` bytes are copied over. So `buffer` and `buffer_index` come up zeroed correctly. Entry point `0x4003a0` is inside the executable range (`0x3a0 <= 0x3d0 - 4`), so `entry_is_executable` passes.

`msh-prompt` only asserts `uart0_contains = "msh> "`, and your loop prints that on the first iteration before any input arrives. So Fix 1 should make it pass.

## The catch

Adding the module isn't enough on its own. The module table in the ROM image is just a **catalog** — it lists what's available. Your kernel decides which one to boot:

```c
static const char module_name[] = "minimum-user";
...
find_module(boot_info, module_name, sizeof(module_name) - 1U);
```

One name, one lookup. So if you add `msh` alongside `minimum-user` and change nothing else, `find_module` still returns `minimum-user` — the nop loop — and you get the same silent failure.

Unused modules cost you nothing at runtime, though: `find_module` only scans the table, and `load_user_module` fills `user_image_pages` for the one module it's handed. An unbooted module is a few hundred bytes of ROM.

## What makes it work here

The wrinkle is that the kernel ELF is shared three ways:

| test | image | module names present |
|---|---|---|
| `msh-*` | `image/build/minimum.img` | whatever `minimum.toml` says |
| `hello` | `tests/hw2/fixtures/hello/build/hw2-hello.img` | `minimum-user` only |
| `devices` | `tests/hw2/fixtures/devices/build/hw2-devices.img` | `minimum-user` only |

So the kernel can't *unconditionally* require `msh` — hello and devices don't package it, and you shouldn't edit those fixtures. A **fallback chain** satisfies all three:

```c
static const struct minemu_module_record *module =
    find_module(boot_info, "msh", sizeof("msh") - 1U);
if (module == NULL) {
    module = find_module(boot_info, "minimum-user", sizeof("minimum-user") - 1U);
}
```

- `minimum.img` → contains `msh` → boots the shell
- `hw2-hello.img` → no `msh` → falls through → boots hello
- `hw2-devices.img` → no `msh` → falls through → boots devices

Then `image/minimum.toml`:

```toml
kernel = "../kernel/build/minimum-kernel.elf"

[[modules]]
name = "minimum-user"
elf = "../user/prog/minimum-user/build/minimum-user.elf"

[[modules]]
name = "msh"
elf = "../user/prog/msh/build/msh.elf"
```

`find_module` already validates its bounds (`image_records_valid` on the table, `image_range_valid` on each name), so iterating more modules needs no new safety work.

You'd still want the `image/Makefile` change from before — `USER_INPUTS`/`USER_PROGRAM` currently only track `minimum-user`, so edits to `msh/main.c` wouldn't rebuild the image and you'd be debugging stale bytes.

## Which to pick

The two-module version costs you a five-line kernel change and keeps `minimum-user` bootable as a fallback. The one-line version (repoint `minimum-user`'s `elf` at `msh.elf`, keep the name) is less code but leaves `user/prog/minimum-user` dead weight in the build.

Worth weighing: **hw3 needs multi-module images anyway.** The fixture above boots `hw3-process`, which forks and then `exec("hw3-process-target")` — the second module exists purely so user code can exec it by name. If you're heading into fork/exec, getting comfortable with a multi-module manifest now isn't throwaway work; you'll be adding a third or fourth `[[modules]]` block soon regardless.

One thing I'd *not* do: rename the shell's module to something the fixtures also use. The whole reason hello and devices keep working is that they own the name `minimum-user` in their own images — give your shell that same name and you collide with them.

## Why here, and why nothing else moves

Three properties of the surrounding code make this spot work:

**`find_module` needs no changes.** It's already a pure lookup that returns `NULL` on miss (`main.c:150-170`), and it re-validates the module table on every call via `image_records_valid`. Calling it twice is safe — the table is in ROM, unmodified between calls. The second call just scans one or two more entries.

**It must resolve *before* `load_user_module`, not interleave with it.** `load_user_module` mutates shared state — it zeroes `user_page_table`, resets `user_page_count`, and fills `user_image_pages`. So you have to settle on one module first and load exactly once. Trying to "load and see if it works" would leave you with a half-populated address space on a miss.

**`module` stays the single source for both consumers.** Line 459 loads it, and line 463 enters it:

```c
minemu_enter_user(module->entry_vaddr, USER_STACK_TOP);
```

The fallback reassigns the same variable, so `entry_vaddr` comes from whichever record actually won. Easy to get wrong if you split it into two separate `module` pointers.

## One consequence worth knowing

Order decides priority: **msh wins if both are packaged.** That's what you want for `minimum.img`, where both names will be present. It only becomes a hazard if you ever package `msh` into a fixture image that's supposed to boot something else — then msh silently shadows it. Unlikely to bite, but now you know why.

## And don't add hw3's target to this chain

When you get to fork/exec, `tests/hw3/fixtures/process/image.toml` packages a second module, `hw3-process-target`, purely so user code can reach it via `exec("hw3-process-target")`. Those names resolve through the exec path, not at boot — the kernel only ever *boots* one module. Adding target names to the boot fallback chain would make the kernel boot the target directly and break the test's expectation that the parent runs first. Keep this chain strictly about "what do we boot."

If you later want more than two candidates, a name array with a small loop reads better than a nested chain — but for two names the `if` is clearer. And since hw3 only ever boots one module, you may never need the array.

## What works

`image/build/minimum.img` now carries both modules, and the kernel looks for `"msh"`, which it finds. So `msh-prompt`, `msh-echo`, `msh-editing`, `msh-overlong` will boot your shell. Also `minimum.toml` is already a prerequisite of `$(IMAGE)` (`image/Makefile:33`), so the image rebuilds on its own — no manual clean needed.

## What breaks

The kernel ELF is shared with the hw2 fixture images, and both of those package **only** `"minimum-user"`:

```
tests/hw2/fixtures/hello/image.toml   → name = "minimum-user", elf = hw2-hello.elf
tests/hw2/fixtures/devices/image.toml → name = "minimum-user", elf = hw2-devices.elf
```

Neither contains a module named `"msh"`. Your kernel at `main.c:444` now searches for exactly one name with no fallback, so on those images:

```c
find_module(...) → NULL
    → module == NULL → trace 0xb007bad1 → minemu_fail_stop()
```

It dies at boot before ever entering user mode. You'll get the same `UART0 output did not contain expected text` failure, but for a completely different reason than last time — now it's a hard hang, not a nop loop.

You traded two passing tests for four passing tests. Net loss of one, and a silent one at that.

## The fix

Add the fallback you skipped. It's five lines at `main.c:457-458`:

```c
    static const char shell_module[] = "msh";
    static const char fallback_module[] = "minimum-user";
    ...
    const struct minemu_module_record *module =
        find_module(boot_info, shell_module, sizeof(shell_module) - 1U);
    if (module == NULL) {
        module = find_module(boot_info, fallback_module,
                             sizeof(fallback_module) - 1U);
    }
```

That covers all three images: `minimum.img` has `msh` so it boots the shell; the two fixture images lack `msh`, fall through, and boot `minimum-user`. Keep your two-module `minimum.toml` exactly as it is — it's already correct.

If you'd rather not carry two names, the alternative is to revert line 444 to `"minimum-user"` and point that module's `elf` at `msh.elf` — one name, no fallback. But then your two-module manifest collapses back to one and `user/prog/minimum-user` is dead weight. Given you've chosen to keep both, the fallback is the consistent option.

## Still outstanding

`image/Makefile:5,14-21,30-31` tracks only `minimum-user`. Your image rebuilt just now because `minimum.toml` changed — but from here on, editing `user/prog/msh/main.c` will **not** trigger an image rebuild. You'll be testing stale bytes, and that's a genuinely painful thing to debug. Point `USER_PROGRAM` at `msh.elf` and widen `USER_INPUTS` to `../user/prog/msh/*` before you do anything else.

## One regression to decide on

`tests/hw1/*.toml` also boot `image/build/minimum.img`. `hw1/hello-world.toml` asserts `uart0_contains = "hello world"`, which used to come from the `cprintf("hello world\n")` at the top of your commented-out kernel shell. Your `msh` program doesn't print that, so hw1's hello-world test will now fail.

If you still need hw1 green, `msh` can emit `"hello world\n"` before its first prompt — `uart0_contains` is a substring check, so that satisfies hw1 without disturbing `msh-prompt`. If hw1 is behind you, ignore it. Only you know whether that regression matters, but it's worth being deliberate about rather than discovering it later.

## Defects I did find

**1. `image/Makefile:32-34` — broken recipe (real bug)**

```make
$(USER_PROGRAM): $(USER_INPUTS)
	$(MAKE) -C ../user/prog/minimum-user all \
	$(MAKE) -C ../user/prog/msh all
```

The trailing `\` joins these into one command: `make -C .../minimum-user all make -C .../msh all`. The second `-C` resolves relative to `minimum-user`, i.e. `user/prog/prog/msh` — nonexistent. It only survives today because the root `image:` target builds `user` first, so these targets are always already up to date and the recipe never runs. It will break the moment someone invokes `make -C image` standalone. Fix: two separate recipe lines.

**2. hw1 `hello-world` regression** — `main.c:469` has `cprintf("hello world\n")` commented out, but `tests/hw1/hello-world.toml:6` asserts `uart0_contains = "hello world"`. A substring check tolerates printing it before the first `msh> `.

**3. Dead code** at `main.c:43-64`, `468-502`, plus `static volatile bool newline` and `MAX_LINE_LENGTH`.

**4. The `msh` fallback is correct and must stay** — I confirmed `tests/hw2/fixtures/{hello,devices}/image.toml` package only `"minimum-user"`, so dropping the fallback would re-break both.

## The one structural difference worth flagging

| | `hw2-hello` (works) | `msh` (fails) |
|---|---|---|
| sections | `.text` only | `.text` + `.rodata` + `.bss` |
| segment flags | `0x5` (R E) | `0x7` (**RWE**) |
| `filesz` vs `memsz` | equal | `0x3d0` < `0x3ec` |

Your `msh` is the first user program that forces a **writable** user page and a **`.bss` zero-fill tail**. Neither `hello` nor `devices` exercised that. Note the irony: `write_string("msh> ")` only *reads* `.rodata`, so "msh> " should print before any `.bss` write — meaning a permissions fault shouldn't preempt it. That paradox is exactly why I want runtime signal rather than another hypothesis.

## Plan

**Step 1 — Make the kernel observable (highest value, ~2 minutes).**
Add a distinct trace event at each stage in `kernel/src/core/main.c`:
- `0x600d0001` right after `find_module("msh")` returns non-NULL (so we see whether "msh" was found, or the fallback silently fired)
- `0x600d0002` after `load_user_module` succeeds
- `0x600d0003` immediately before `minemu_enter_user`

Then run against a **diagnostic copy** of the manifest, not the real one — `tests/hw2/msh-prompt.toml` is a test manifest, not a `tests/hw2/fixtures/*` manifest, but a `/tmp` copy keeps it clean:

```toml
# /tmp/msh-diag.toml  — same as msh-prompt.toml plus:
[assert]
trace_values = [0x600d0001, 0x600d0002, 0x600d0003]
```

This bisects the whole boot path in one run and answers the only question that matters:
- **No `...0001`** → `find_module("msh")` failed; the fallback hid it. Look at name matching / `module_count`.
- **`...0001` but no `...0002`** → `load_user_module` rejected the RWE segment or the `.bss` tail. Isolate the flags/`memsz` path.
- **All three, still no `"msh> "`** → the kernel is fine and the fault is inside `msh` itself (entry stub, `.rodata` read, or `ioctl` marshalling).

**Step 2 — Fix per the result.** Most likely branch is the third; if so, the cheapest isolation is a minimal `msh` that does `write_string("msh> ")` then `bkpt #0`, with the buffers made stack-locals instead of `static` — that removes `.bss`, drops the segment to `0x5`, and matches the known-good `hello` shape exactly. If that prints, add the statics back one at a time.

**Step 3 — Independent of the above, the defects I already found that need fixing regardless:**
1. `image/Makefile:32-34` — the `\`-joined recipe runs `make -C .../minimum-user all make -C .../msh all` as one command; the second `-C` resolves to the nonexistent `user/prog/prog/msh`. Works today only because the root `image:` target pre-builds `user`. Split into two recipe lines.
2. `main.c:469` — `cprintf("hello world\n")` is commented out but `tests/hw1/hello-world.toml:6` asserts `uart0_contains = "hello world"`. Re-enable it before the first `msh> ` prompt; the substring check tolerates it.
3. Delete dead code: `main.c:43-64`, `468-502`, `static volatile bool newline`, `MAX_LINE_LENGTH`.
4. Keep the `"msh"` → `"minimum-user"` fallback — `tests/hw2/fixtures/{hello,devices}/image.toml` package only `"minimum-user"`, so dropping it re-breaks both.

The kernel's second `PT_LOAD` is `filesz=0x1939`, `memsz=0x1c088`. That gap — **108,367 bytes of BSS** — is zeroed by `bootloader/src/boot.c:67` `zero_bytes`, a **byte-at-a-time** loop. That's ~108K iterations of `strb`/`add`/`cmp`/`bne` ≈ **433K instructions**, before the kernel even starts.

The rest of the fixed boot cost:

| work | bytes | ~instructions |
|---|---|---|
| bootloader BSS zero | 108,367 | 433K |
| bootloader `copy_bytes` | 6,457 | 39K |
| `boot.S` map loops | — | 60K |
| `map_system_rom` table zero | 16,384 | 65K |
| `load_user_module` zeros | 8,192 | 33K |

**≈ 630K instructions**, plus fetch overhead. That lands exactly where the evidence says: `hello` passes at `1M`, `msh-prompt` fails at `700K`, and `50M` is comfortable. It's a knife-edge, and `msh` is just barely over.

## The hw1 wrinkle

`cprintf("hello world\n")` sits at `main.c:470` — **after** `minemu_enter_user(...)` at line 468, which is `__attribute__((noreturn))`. Uncommenting it in place leaves it unreachable; it would still never print. Restoring hw1 `hello-world` means moving the call **above** `minemu_enter_user`, so it prints on every boot before user mode.

That's compatible with hw2 — the assertions are substring matches, so `"hello world\nmsh> msh> worked fine\n..."` still contains every expected `msh` substring. But note `tests/hw1/hello-world.toml:3` is `max_ticks = 500000` — **tighter** than msh-prompt's 700000. So this only works because of the tick fix below. The two items aren't independent.

## The tick fix, precisely

`kernel/src/core/main.c:30`:
```c
static uint8_t user_image_pages[MAX_USER_IMAGE_PAGES][MINEMU_PAGE_SIZE];
```
`16 × 4096 = 65,536` bytes — **60% of the kernel's 108,367-byte BSS**. The bootloader zeroes that BSS one byte at a time (`bootloader/src/boot.c:67`), ~4 instructions per byte ≈ **433K instructions** before the kernel starts.

`MAX_USER_IMAGE_PAGES` 16 → 4 removes 49,152 bytes ≈ **196K instructions**. Boot drops from ~630K to **~435K** — under both msh-prompt's 700K and hw1's 500K.

Every module in the repo loads in exactly 1 page (`msh` needs `memsz=0x3ec`), so 4 pages keeps 4× headroom. The only cost is capping a user module at 16KB instead of 64KB.

## Plan

**1. `kernel/src/core/main.c:20`** — `#define MAX_USER_IMAGE_PAGES 4U`

**2. `kernel/src/core/main.c`** — move `cprintf("hello world\n");` from the dead block to just before `minemu_enter_user(...)` at line 468. Preserve its original position relative to `uart_init()` — it printed *before* init in the working hw1 code, so don't reorder that.

**3. `image/Makefile:32-34`** — the trailing `\` joins two commands into one:
```make
$(MAKE) -C ../user/prog/minimum-user all \
$(MAKE) -C ../user/prog/msh all
```
The second `-C` resolves relative to `minimum-user`, i.e. the nonexistent `user/prog/prog/msh`. It survives today only because the root `image:` target pre-builds `user`, so this recipe never runs. Split into two recipe lines.

**4. Delete dead code** — the commented `uart_handler` block (`43-64`), the commented shell (`469-507`), `static volatile bool newline` (`39`, and its only other uses are inside the block being deleted), `#define MAX_LINE_LENGTH` (`15`), and the commented `buffer`/`buffer_index` (`37-38`). Verify `memcpy`/`memcmp`/`uart_init`/`minemu_irq_enable` still resolve after removal — if they were only used by the deleted block, the corresponding includes may also be droppable.

**5. Keep** the `"msh"` → `"minimum-user"` fallback. `tests/hw2/fixtures/{hello,devices}/image.toml` package only `"minimum-user"`; dropping it re-breaks both.

## Verification order

Run these after rebuilding the image — each gates the next:

1. `just test hw2 msh-prompt` at the **original** 700000. This is the real test; don't keep the raised value.
2. `just test hw2 hello` and `just test hw2 devices` — must stay green (they exercise the fallback).
3. `just test hw2 editing` — settles the open question of whether `uart0_contains` normalizes whitespace. If it fails on `worked   fine` vs `worked fine`, `msh`'s echo needs to re-tokenize arguments with single separators.
4. `just test hw2 echo`, `just test hw2 overlong` — overlong still needs the drop-the-entire-line behavior.
5. `just test hw1 hello-world` at its 500000 — the tightest budget in the set.

## The trace

```

`uart0_contains` is a substring check, and `"worked   fine"` does not contain `"worked fine"`. Line 3 (`command not found: bogus`) traces correctly — it already truncates at the first space, so it's unaffected. The whitespace is the *only* divergence in this test.

## Two more failures I found by tracing ahead

Worth catching now rather than one test at a time.

**`msh-echo` will fail next.** Its input is `"echo hello from user mode"` — **25 characters**. Your `MAX_LINE_LENGTH` is `20`, so the buffer truncates to `"echo hello from use"` and echoes `"hello from use"`. Expected is `"hello from user mode"`. The limit has to be ≥ 25.

**`msh-overlong` will fail after that.** Input is 160 `a`s. Current code ignores the surplus, keeps 20, and prints `command not found: aaaa...`. The test expects `"msh> msh> "` — meaning the overlong line must produce **zero output**, just two consecutive prompts. That needs an explicit overflow flag; dropping characters silently isn't enough.

## Plan — all three fixes in `user/prog/msh/main.c`

**1. Raise `MAX_LINE_LENGTH` 20 → 64.** Must satisfy `>= 25` (echo) and `< 160` (overlong). 64 sits comfortably between. It grows the user module's `.bss` by ~44 bytes, still far inside the single page, so no change to the 4-page limit.

**2. Add an `overflow` flag.** Set it when a printable char arrives at a full buffer; clear it at line start. On `'\n'`, if set, skip processing entirely — no echo, no `command not found` — so the shell just re-prompts.

**3. Replace `write_string(arg)` with whitespace-normalizing echo.** Split on runs of spaces, emit each word, and emit exactly one space *between* words — none before the first, none after the last. That also handles the trailing `"fine  "` in the editing input.

```

which matches the assertion exactly, character for character.

```c
#include <stdint.h>
#include "minemu/user_abi.h"
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>

#define MAX_WORD_LENGTH 20

static char word[MAX_WORD_LENGTH + 1];
static size_t word_index = 0;
static bool overflow = false;
static bool command_resolved = false;
static bool echo_mode = false;
static bool echo_started = false;
static bool line_output = false;

static void write_bytes(const char *str, size_t length) {
    ioctl(MINEMU_FD_UART_OUT, MINEMU_IOCTL_UART_WRITE, str, length);
}

static void write_string(const char *str) {
    size_t length = 0;
    while (str[length] != '\0') ++length;
    write_bytes(str, length);
}

static void line_reset(void) {
    word_index = 0;
    overflow = false;
    command_resolved = false;
    echo_mode = false;
    echo_started = false;
    line_output = false;
}

static void finish_word(bool line_end) {
    word[word_index] = '\0';
    size_t length = word_index;
    word_index = 0;

    if (overflow) {
        /* Line is too long: discard it entirely. */
        if (line_end) line_reset();
        return;
    }

    if (!command_resolved) {
        command_resolved = true;
        if (length == 4 && word[0]=='e' && word[1]=='c' && word[2]=='h' && word[3]=='o') {
            echo_mode = true;
        } else if (length != 0) {
            write_string("command not found: ");
            write_bytes(word, length);
            line_output = true;
        }
    } else if (echo_mode && length != 0) {
        if (echo_started) write_string(" ");
        echo_started = true;
        write_bytes(word, length);
        line_output = true;
    }

    if (line_end) {
        if (line_output) write_string("\n");
        line_reset();
    }
}
```
